planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; strongest coloring and the longest weeping leaves develop under high light.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Majesticum is a distinctive weeping croton with long, slender, drooping leaves marked by a yellow midrib that deepens to red as the leaf matures, giving established plants a cascading, fountain-like silhouette very different from the stiffer, upright habit of broad-leaved cultivars. The pendulous branching makes it well suited to elevated planters, large hanging baskets, or as a soft textural accent among bolder tropical foliage. Bright light is essential for holding the vivid vein coloring; plants in low light revert toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries, wear gloves when pruning since the milky sap is a skin and eye irritant, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Codiaeum variegatum

common_name: Franklin Roosevelt Croton (Narrow Curly Maroon-Splashed Croton)

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; the paint-splashed coloring is strongest under high light.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Franklin Roosevelt is a narrow-leaved, heirloom croton named as a companion to the similarly styled 'Eleanor Roosevelt', with long, arching, pointed leaves splashed in yellow, orange, and pink over medium green and backed in red, the oldest leaves darkening to deep burgundy-maroon with age. The dramatic color progression from lime-flecked new growth to near-black older foliage gives a single plant several distinct looks at once. Bright light develops and holds the strongest splashed coloring; plants in lower light fade toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries, handle cuttings carefully since the sap is an irritant, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden — Codiaeum variegatum var. pictum 'Franklin Roosevelt'

planting.note: Plant container plants after the last frost in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light; steady soil moisture and high light keep the color progression consistent.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Red Iceton is a sport of the older 'Mrs. Iceton' with broad, pointed oval leaves that emerge a bright warm yellow and shade progressively into red and pink as each leaf ages, so a well-grown plant carries yellow, orange, and deep red foliage simultaneously. Keep soil evenly moist rather than allowing it to swing between wet and dry, since Codiaeum drops leaves in response to both extremes. Bright light is needed to trigger the full yellow-to-red color shift; low light plants stall out mostly green. Wear gloves when pruning, since the milky sap is a skin and eye irritant, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, or grow as a houseplant in bright light. Andreanum is a classic broadleaf croton in the Croton Society's 'broad leaf' cultivar group, with large oval leaves up to ten inches long colored yellow-green with prominent gold veins and margins, a bolder and more solid-colored look than the narrow, speckled, or curled types. Its substantial leaf size and strong architectural form make it a good specimen or anchor plant in a tropical foliage bed. Bright light develops and holds the strongest gold veining; plants in lower light fade toward plain green. Water when the top inch of soil dries, keep the irritating milky sap away from skin and eyes when pruning, and protect from any frost, since croton has no cold tolerance.
